CHIEF COMPLAINT
Referral from emergency room for evaluation of esophagitis; chest pain three months ago that has resolved.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a new patient referred from the emergency room. Three months ago in early October, patient experienced chest pain that began randomly and lasted approximately four days. Pain was described as sharp, located in the center of the chest behind the breastbone, and felt like a heart attack. Pain was worse with eating. Patient also experienced difficulty swallowing during this time. After four days of pain, patient went to the emergency room because nothing relieved it. ER evaluation included EKG and blood tests, all of which were normal. Cardiac workup was normal. The emergency room attributed symptoms to a GI etiology and referred patient to gastroenterology. Both chest pain and swallowing difficulty resolved approximately three days after the ER visit. Patient has been asymptomatic since that time. Patient denies having heartburn or indigestion during the episode and is unsure what heartburn feels like. Patient notes she was going through a stressful job transition around the time the chest pain occurred. Patient has been trying to lose weight. Denies abdominal pain. Bowel movements are normal.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies family history of GI problems. No other symptoms discussed.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Uterine fibroids, anemia, cholecystectomy several years ago.

MEDICATIONS
Not discussed.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient denies awareness of family history of GI problems.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient was going through a stressful job transition around the time of the chest pain episode three months ago. Patient has been trying to lose weight.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: Lower abdomen without pain or tenderness. Upper abdomen with mild tenderness to light palpation in the upper abdominal quadrants, symmetric. Exam otherwise normal and appears good.

RESULTS
ER EKG: normal. ER blood tests: normal. Cardiac workup: normal.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Differential diagnosis includes anxiety, esophagitis, GERD, dyspepsia, and musculoskeletal etiologies. Suspect patient had an anxiety attack related to her job transition with possible contribution from musculoskeletal etiologies. Since symptoms occurred three months ago and patient has been asymptomatic since that time, if esophagitis were present it would likely have already healed and would not be visible on endoscopy. Discussed EGD (upper endoscopy) versus monitoring for symptoms. Patient elected to self-monitor symptoms and will call the office if additional episodes of pain or other concerning symptoms develop. If symptoms recur, patient will be scheduled for EGD. Patient to follow up as needed for any other GI complaints.
